clue.text: Speaking likeness of Galatea

parts.note: Galatea was the carved maiden Pygmalion made, a lifelike figure that came to life, so a 'speaking likeness' in two senses

explanation.surface: A description of a vivid portrait of the sea-nymph or Pygmalion's beloved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Speaking likeness' is a phrase for a lifelike portrait; here Galatea was literally a carved figure that came alive and could speak.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Pygmalion myth Galatea began as a carved ivory sculpture, a likeness that was then given life.

clue.text: "There are no faces than those that are so wash'd " (Much Ado About Nothing)

definitions.text: There are no faces than those that are so wash'd

parts.words: There are no faces than those that are so wash'd
parts.note: a line from Leonato in Much Ado About Nothing with one word left out, which the solver supplies: faces washed with tears are the most honest

explanation.surface: A Shakespeare quotation with a gap, from the opening scene of Much Ado About Nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: A literary fill-in: the missing comparative completes Leonato's line about faces washed with tears of joy; the gap itself is not marked in the clue as printed.
explanation.definitionFit: The line says tear-washed faces are the most sincere, so the gap wants the comparative of 'faithful' or 'honest'.

clue.text: Master Shallow also heard them at midnight

definitions.text: Master Shallow also heard them at midnight

parts.words: Master Shallow also heard them at midnight
parts.note: Falstaff tells Justice Shallow in Henry IV Part 2 that they have heard the bells ring at midnight; the title of a Dickens Christmas book too, hence 'also'

explanation.surface: Falstaff reminiscing with his old friend about late nights in their youth.
explanation.walkthrough: Falstaff's line 'We have heard the chimes at midnight, Master Shallow' gives the phrase; 'also' nods to the Dickens Christmas story of that title.
explanation.definitionFit: The bells striking twelve are what Falstaff and Shallow recall hearing on their wild nights at Clement's Inn.

clue.text: Darkness to be traversed, before getting public transport?

parts.note: ere is the poetic word for before
a bus is a common form of public transport

explanation.surface: A traveller facing a dark stretch before catching a bus home.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth this is the primeval darkness the dead pass through on the way to Hades, hence 'to be traversed'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek mythology Erebus is the personification of darkness and the shadowy region souls cross into the underworld.

clue.text: Part of joint including New York's poet

indicators.note: the joint part takes the New York abbreviation inside it, so including signals a container

parts.note: a tenon is the projecting piece of a mortise-and-tenon joint in carpentry
NY is the abbreviation for New York, plus the S of the possessive

explanation.surface: A carpentry joint somehow linked to a New York poet.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'S of 'New York's' is used as a letter here, not dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred, Lord Tennyson was Victorian Poet Laureate, author of In Memoriam and The Charge of the Light Brigade.

clue.text: Coxed pair? (to say nothing of the dog)

definitions.text: Coxed pair? (to say nothing of the dog)

parts.words: Coxed pair? (to say nothing of the dog)
parts.note: a rowing crew of two oarsmen plus a cox makes three people afloat, and the bracket is the subtitle of Jerome K. Jerome's comic novel

explanation.surface: A rowing term, with a jokey aside about a dog coming along too.
explanation.walkthrough: A coxed pair is a boat with two rowers and a coxswain, three people in all; Jerome K. Jerome's novel carries the subtitle 'To Say Nothing of the Dog'.
explanation.definitionFit: Jerome's comic novel follows three friends rowing up the Thames, exactly the number in a coxed pair.

clue.text: Role like Moll Flanders or Fanny Hill

definitions.text: Role like Moll Flanders or Fanny Hill

parts.words: Role like Moll Flanders or Fanny Hill
parts.note: both novels are titled after their heroine, so in a stage or film version the lead character's name is the title

explanation.surface: A casting call for one of two notorious eighteenth-century heroines.
explanation.walkthrough: Defoe's Moll Flanders and Cleland's Fanny Hill are both named for their heroine, so either lead would be the title role.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatre term for the title role, the character whose name a play or novel bears.

clue.text: Novelist, something of a lawyer by profession ()

indicators.note: only a part of the following words is taken, so the name sits inside them

explanation.surface: A writer who once practised some law.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Something of' takes a run of letters from 'lawyer by'; Frank Yerby was an American historical novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Frank Yerby was an American writer of bestselling historical romances such as The Foxes of Harrow.

clue.text: His life was enough to shame the devil

definitions.text: His life was enough to shame the devil

parts.words: His life was enough to shame the devil
parts.note: the Irish writer Liam ... called his 1934 autobiography Shame the Devil

explanation.surface: A remark about a man whose wicked life outdid Satan himself.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a sinner; in fact 'Shame the Devil' is the title of the Irish novelist Liam O'Flaherty's memoir, so his 'life' (story) was that book.
explanation.definitionFit: Liam O'Flaherty, author of The Informer, published his autobiography under the title Shame the Devil.

clue.text: Somehow agree a menu for Bulwer Lytton's schoolmaster

indicators.note: the letters are put together in some other way, so the phrase is rearranged

explanation.surface: Settling on a menu for a novelist's teacher.
explanation.definitionFit: Bulwer-Lytton's 1832 novel tells of a real Knaresborough schoolmaster who was hanged for murder.

clue.text: Eric Linklater's was of honour

parts.note: the Scottish novelist Eric Linklater wrote a novel called ... of Honour, so the missing noun completes that title

explanation.surface: A remark on the military honours of a Scottish writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Linklater was a Scottish novelist; the clue completes the title of his 1961 novel about war dead.
explanation.definitionFit: A list of names, such as of those who died in war, is the noun that precedes 'of honour'.

clue.text: Beethoven trio badly received in Sarajevo?

definitions.meaning: Beethoven's Piano Trio Op. 97 is named after its dedicatee
Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austrian throne, was assassinated on his 1914 visit to Sarajevo

explanation.surface: A piece of chamber music that went down poorly in Bosnia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badly received' reads as a poor concert review, but refers to the shooting of Franz Ferdinand in 1914.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of a Habsburg prince: Beethoven's patron Rudolph and the murdered Franz Ferdinand both held it.

clue.text: Deceptive bid from Beaumont and Shadwell

definitions.meaning: in bridge, a psychic bid misrepresents one's hand to mislead opponents
Joseph Beaumont wrote a long poem and Thomas Shadwell an opera, both titled after Cupid's beloved

explanation.surface: A bluff in an auction involving two seventeenth-century writers.
explanation.walkthrough: In contract bridge a deliberately misleading call is a 'psych' or psyche; Beaumont's poem (1648) and Shadwell's opera (1675) share the title.
explanation.definitionFit: Bridge slang for a bluffing call, and the name of the girl loved by Cupid in the myth both writers retold.

clue.text: The Annales Cambriae are partly a swindle

indicators.note: only part of the Latin title is used, so the word lies within it

explanation.surface: A claim that the medieval Welsh chronicle is in part a fraud.
explanation.walkthrough: The Annales Cambriae are medieval Welsh annals; the answer runs across the join of the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A confidence trick or fraud that cheats someone of money.

clue.text: That of Richards was practical

parts.note: I. A. Richards, the Cambridge critic, published Practical ... in 1929, so the missing noun completes that title

explanation.surface: Someone praising a man named Richards for being down-to-earth.
explanation.walkthrough: I. A. Richards's book Practical Criticism founded close reading of poems; 'practical' reads as a personal trait.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun for literary judgement and analysis, the subject of Richards's famous book.

clue.text: Go wrong with worker on railway in search for adventure

parts.note: to err is to make a mistake
the worker ant is a crossword's stock worker

explanation.surface: A railway employee who has lost his way while seeking excitement.
explanation.definitionFit: The knight-errant's way of life was roaming in quest of adventures, as in chivalric romance.

clue.text: Stout fellow (emperor, novelist)

parts.note: Nero was the Roman emperor said to have fiddled while Rome burned
Thomas Wolfe was the American author of Look Homeward, Angel

explanation.surface: A portly man described in brackets as both emperor and writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stout fellow' sounds like a sturdy chap or a fat one; it means a character created by Rex Stout, his corpulent orchid-growing detective.
explanation.definitionFit: Rex Stout's famous fat New York detective is the creation the clue calls a 'Stout fellow'.

clue.text: It's better to be — than honest " (Tom Stoppard)

definitions.text: It's better to be — than honest " (Tom Stoppard)

parts.words: It's better to be — than honest " (Tom Stoppard)
parts.note: a line from Stoppard's play Travesties with one word blanked, to be supplied by the solver

explanation.surface: A witty quotation from a modern playwright, with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap is filled by the adjective for something that is worth citing; the line is from Stoppard's Travesties.
explanation.definitionFit: Stoppard's joke prefers being worth citing to being truthful, so the gap needs a word for fit to be repeated.

clue.text: Twins in radio's curious item

indicators.note: the answer is found inside the words that follow, so in signals the letters lie within them

explanation.surface: A broadcast story about a curious pair of twins.
explanation.walkthrough: The name straddles 'radio's' and 'curious'; the Dioscuri are Castor and Pollux, the twin sons of Zeus.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the Dioscuri are Castor and Pollux, twin brothers later placed among the stars as Gemini.

clue.text: Jean starts Rochester's history, yet stops

indicators.note: the beginnings of the next four words are taken, so starts signals picking first letters

explanation.surface: A woman begins telling Rochester's story, then breaks off.
explanation.walkthrough: Jean Rhys wrote Wide Sargasso Sea, the history of Mr Rochester's first wife from Jane Eyre, so the surface fits the author.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean Rhys is the Dominican-born novelist, so her first name stands for her surname here.

clue.text: "I am as melancholy as a —, or a lugg'd bear" (Henry IV, Part I)

definitions.text: "I am as melancholy as a —, or a lugg'd bear" (Henry IV, Part I)

parts.words: "I am as melancholy as a —, or a lugg'd bear" (Henry IV, Part I)
parts.note: Falstaff's line to Prince Hal with one word blanked: the animal is a castrated tomcat, proverbially sad

explanation.surface: Falstaff complaining of his gloom, with a word missing from the quotation.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'gib' is an old word for a castrated male cat, thought to be listless and melancholy; a 'lugg'd bear' is a baited bear dragged by the ears.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic term for a gelded tomcat, which Falstaff names as a byword for gloom.

clue.text: Song included by Joyce Oates ()

definitions.meaning: a festive hymn, as sung at Christmas
the American novelist's full name has a middle name between Joyce and Oates

explanation.surface: A song that a novelist put into one of her books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Included by' seems to mean she quoted a song; in fact the word sits within her name, Joyce Carol Oates.
explanation.definitionFit: A joyful hymn, especially at Christmas, and also the middle name of the novelist Joyce Carol Oates.

clue.text: First man on fish-trap in Stevenson book

parts.note: Adam was the first man in Genesis
a weir is a fence set in a river to trap fish

explanation.surface: The original man perched on a river trap, in a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' puts the fish-trap after the first man in a down sense; the character is the hanging judge in Stevenson's unfinished Weir of Hermiston.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Hermiston, the harsh judge in Robert Louis Stevenson's last novel Weir of Hermiston, bears this name.

clue.text: Oscar's sort of mate ()

parts.note: Oscar Wilde wrote the comedy An ... Husband, and a husband is a mate, so the word is the adjective in that title

explanation.surface: Asking what kind of partner someone named Oscar would want.
explanation.walkthrough: Oscar is Wilde; his play An Ideal Husband gives the adjective, with 'mate' standing for husband.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilde's play title describes the perfect spouse, and a spouse is a mate.

clue.text: Billy, undertaker's clerk addicted to pork pies

definitions.text: Billy, undertaker's clerk addicted to pork pies

parts.words: Billy, undertaker's clerk addicted to pork pies
parts.note: Billy Fisher in Keith Waterhouse's novel works for undertakers and tells constant 'pork pies', rhyming slang for lies

explanation.surface: A funeral clerk with a weakness for meat pies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pork pies' is British rhyming slang for lies. Billy Fisher, hero of Keith Waterhouse's Billy ___, is a fantasist clerk at an undertaker's.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who tells untruths habitually, as Waterhouse's daydreaming hero does, which gives the novel its title.

clue.text: A generous, liberal-minded man, according to Dr Johnson

definitions.text: A generous, liberal-minded man, according to Dr Johnson

parts.words: A generous, liberal-minded man, according to Dr Johnson
parts.note: Johnson, himself the son of a book trader, praised those who sell books as generous, liberal-minded men

explanation.surface: Samuel Johnson's description of a kindly and open-minded fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: Boswell records Johnson saying that the men who sold books were generous, liberal-minded men.
explanation.definitionFit: Johnson praised the book trade, whose dealers paid authors and published his Dictionary.

clue.text: Tobias Smelfungus, Doctor of Men and Manners

definitions.text: Tobias Smelfungus, Doctor of Men and Manners

parts.words: Tobias Smelfungus, Doctor of Men and Manners
parts.note: Sterne mocked the Scottish novelist Tobias, a trained surgeon and grumpy travel writer, as Smelfungus in A Sentimental Journey

explanation.surface: An imagined title for a sour physician who studied society.
explanation.walkthrough: Sterne's nickname 'Smelfungus' targeted the author of Travels through France and Italy; he had trained as a ship's surgeon and wrote novels of manners such as Humphry Clinker.
explanation.definitionFit: Tobias Smollett, novelist and surgeon, was the travel writer Sterne dubbed Smelfungus.

clue.text: Goading for Hodge in early play

definitions.meaning: provocation or persistent irritation, as a noun
in Gammer Gurton's ..., an early English comedy, the lost sewing tool is being used to mend Hodge's breeches

explanation.surface: Teasing a farmhand in an old comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: Gammer Gurton's Needle (c.1550s) is one of the first English comedies; Gammer loses the tool while patching her servant Hodge's breeches.
explanation.definitionFit: Provocation is called this in British usage, and it is the lost sewing tool in Gammer Gurton's comedy.
